---
title: "Declaring an asset"
---

```{python}
#| label: setup-declaring-an-asset
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: import `OrdersSchema` from `dd.data`, which the examples on this page use"
#| output: false
import dagster as dg
import polars as pl

import dagster_dataframely as dd
from dagster_dataframely.data import OrdersSchema
```

Use `dd.asset` in place of `@dg.asset` on a function that returns a Polars frame.
This page covers its arguments, the code version it derives from the schema, and what the decorated function may return.
The schema is the only required argument, and it is positional.
Every other argument is `filter`, `error_rows_key` or `error_rows_io_manager_key` ([Filtering error rows](filtering-error-rows.qmd)), one of the [Settings](settings.qmd), or a `@dg.asset` parameter under the same name.

You write the decorated function as you would for `@dg.asset`:

```{python}
#| label: declaring-an-asset-1
@dd.asset(OrdersSchema, filter=True, group_name="sales")
def orders(context: dg.AssetExecutionContext, raw_orders: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    context.log.info("raw_orders has %d rows", raw_orders.height)
    return raw_orders
```

Dagster passes upstream assets to it by parameter name.
Use `ins=` and `deps=` where a parameter name is not enough.
Declare a `context` parameter to use the partition key, the log, resources or configuration.

## Import time and run time

`dd.asset` builds the asset's definition when the module imports, and validates the frame when the asset runs.

<!-- rumdl-disable-next-line MD078 -->
```{mermaid}
%%| label: declaring-an-asset-diagram
flowchart TB
    subgraph load["when the module imports"]
        D["@dd.asset(OrdersSchema)"] --> T["Columns tab"]
        D --> C["a check spec per rule, plus the column-schema check"]
    end
    subgraph run["when the asset runs"]
        direction TB
        F["decorated function returns a frame"] --> CS["column-schema check"]
        CS --> FL["Schema.filter"]
        FL --> V["the asset's IO manager writes the table"]
        FL --> I["with filter=True, the IO manager writes the error rows"]
        FL --> R["a result per check"]
    end
    load --> run
```

Two things exist as soon as the module imports, before any run:

- **The Columns tab**, built from the schema.
- **A check spec per rule at the default granularity, plus one for the column-schema check**, so the catalog lists the asset's checks by name before the first run.

The asset's description comes from the schema's docstring, as [Naming](naming.qmd) describes.

A run validates the frame the decorated function returns.
[Validation](validation.qmd) lists the five kinds of run and what each one writes.

## The parameters `dd.asset` passes to `@dg.asset`

`dd.asset` passes every `@dg.asset` parameter on under the same name, except the six in this table:

| `@dg.asset` parameter | why it is not here | what to write instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `check_specs` | they come from the schema's rules | nothing |
| `key` | `key_prefix` and `name` set it | `key_prefix=` plus `name=` |
| `output_required` | a run that writes nothing must end the step without an output | nothing |
| `dagster_type` | declined ([#3](https://github.com/ozanozbeker/dagster-dataframely/issues/3)): it runs before the IO manager and cannot set a severity, so it cannot apply the rules' severities | the schema, which this package validates against |
| `is_virtual` | a virtual asset has no function to decorate | nothing |
| `io_manager_def` | `resource_defs` already sets it | `resource_defs={"io_manager": ...}` |

`config_schema` is narrower than Dagster's: it takes only a mapping, not the union of six types that `@dg.asset` accepts.
A type checker rejects the five legacy forms, but nothing rejects them at run time.

`dd.asset` adds the `polars` kind to `kinds`.

## The code version

When you pass no `code_version`, `dd.asset` sets the asset's code version to a sha1 hash of the schema, as dagster-dbt does for a model's SQL:

```{python}
#| label: declaring-an-asset-code-version
orders.get_asset_spec().code_version
```

After a schema edit, Dagster marks the asset stale with the cause "has a new code version" until the asset runs again.

`dd.asset` hashes each column's name and dtype, then each rule's name, severity and expression.
So adding, removing or renaming a column or rule changes the code version.
So does a change to a dtype, a column constraint, a `check=`, a `@dy.rule()` or a severity.
The schema's docstring, column descriptions, `filter`, the [Settings](settings.qmd) and column metadata other than the severity declaration do not.

A `code_version` you pass replaces the derived one unchanged.

**Pass a list, not a set, to a Polars `is_in` in a `check=` or `@dy.rule()`.**
Python orders a set of strings differently in each process, and the hash keeps that order.
So with a set of strings, the code version can change each time the code location starts, with no schema change.

**`dd.asset` derives the code version from the schema alone.**
A change to the decorated function's body leaves it unchanged, so Dagster still reports the asset fresh after one.
To cover the function too, pass your own `code_version` and change it when the function changes.

**A Polars upgrade can change every asset's code version at once.**
The hash uses Polars' serialization of each rule's expression, and Polars documents that format as unstable between versions.
After such an upgrade, Dagster can mark every asset stale with the cause "has a new code version", with no schema change.

Polars cannot serialize a Python function, such as the one `map_elements` calls, unless `cloudpickle` is installed.
Without it, `dd.asset` hashes that rule's expression as text, and the text does not include the function's body.
So a change inside the function leaves the code version unchanged.

## The schema is a single `dy.Schema`, never a `dy.Collection`

Passing a Collection raises `CollectionNotSupportedError` at decoration time.
Declare one asset per member instead, each with the member's own schema.
Then pass them to `dd.build_collection_checks`, which reports the Collection's collection filters as asset checks, as [Collection checks](collection-checks.qmd) shows.

The parts under [Hand-wiring](hand-wiring.qmd) cannot validate a Collection either, because `stream_results` takes a single schema.

## What the decorated function returns

The decorated function can return one of five types:

```text
pl.DataFrame                dg.MaterializeResult[pl.DataFrame]
pl.LazyFrame                dg.MaterializeResult[pl.LazyFrame]
None
```

**The returned value determines what happens, not the annotation.**
`@dg.asset` enforces its return annotation, because it infers the output's `dagster_type` from it.
`dd.asset` does not.
The IO manager always receives a `DataFrame`, because `dd.asset` collects a returned `LazyFrame`, as [`LazyFrame`s](lazyframes.qmd) describes.
Annotate the function anyway, so that a type checker enforces the annotation.
Parameterize a returned result, because a strict type checker rejects a bare `dg.MaterializeResult` as an implicit `Any`.

Return a `dg.MaterializeResult` instead of a bare frame when you want to add metadata, tags or a data version to the materialization.
Prefer it to `context.add_asset_metadata`: it is the only one of the two that works when you call the asset directly.
[Attaching your own metadata](what-a-run-produces.qmd#attaching-your-own-metadata) describes both.

Return `None` to skip, as [A partition with no data](partitioning.qmd#a-partition-with-no-data) describes.
To skip, return `None` itself: returning `dg.MaterializeResult(value=None)` raises `MaterializeResultValueError`.

Return anything else and the run fails with `dg.DagsterInvariantViolationError` before the column-schema check.
